The water symbolises Victoria's ‘tsunami of debt’ said to be endangering key services and children View image in fullscreen A screenshot from a Fix Victoria advertisement produced using artificial intelligence. The water symbolises Victoria's ‘tsunami of debt’ said to be endangering key services and children Victorian politics Alarming AI ads are flooding social media in the lead-up to Victoria’s election. But who is behind them? A machete-wielding robber, a ‘tsunami of debt’ … campaigns echoing opposition talking points outspend major parties Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Benita Kolovos and Henry Belot Sat 5 Sep 2026 16.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man clad in a balaclava and brandishing a machete terrorises a worker at a petrol station before firebombing the building on the way out. A woman gives birth on the side of the road, unable to reach a hospital due to ambulance ramping and crater-like potholes, which also stop a fire truck in its tracks. Victorian prisoners to be sent out to repair roads under Labor’s pothole plan Read more A flood of water – emblematic of Victoria’s “tsunami of debt”, forecast to hit $199bn in the next four years – gushes from the steps of state parliament, towards a scared child. These are some of the AI-generated images being used as part of a social media advertising campaign attracting thousands of views less than 100 days out from the Victorian election. According to one expert, the ads, created by a group called Fix Victoria, cost up to $100,000 to publish in August, which is significantly more than most major parties and candidates spent. View image in fullscreen A screenshot from another Fix Victoria ad Another group, Better Victoria, is also spending big on short ads to pit Labor initiatives – such as the multibillion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop – against investment in roads, schools and hospitals. But who is behind these groups and are they affiliated with a political party? ‘Issues-driven, not politics-driven’ Fix Victoria is run by experienced political operatives who held senior positions at a conservative thinktank, the Institute of Public Affairs (IPA). It began plotting its ad campaign in May, when a group of like-minded people started recruiting paying members who could finance its operations and ads. Corporate filings show it was registered with Asic in early August by Deborah Henderson, who was until June the deputy executive director of the IPA. Its communications director is Andrew Hudgson, who held a similar role at the IPA until earlier this year. Its head of advocacy is Gideon Rozner, who spent six years at the IPA before working at an investment firm. Fix Victoria is a separate entity to the IPA and its staff say it is coincidence that three of them previously worked at the thinktank, which is a long-term critic of Labor governments. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In November, Rozner told his social media followers that he was rejoining the Liberal party to support its new leader, Jess Wilson. “The best place for me is to stand with the thousands of Victorians who will get around Jess Wilson to defeat this disgusting Labor government and save the great state of Victoria,” Rozner posted on X. When asked by Guardian Australia whether he is still a member of the Liberal party, Rozner declines to answer but says: “I’ve been around for a long time – and my views and affiliations are well-known.” Rozner says Fix Victoria is an “issues-driven, not politics-driven” organisation that wants to “ensure our leaders know that everyday Victorians want a plan to get out of the mess we are currently in”. “Fix Victoria is focused on the three key issues dragging our state down, that being crime, corruption and debt,” Rozner says. These three issues happen to be key talking points of opposition parties. “Victoria’s tsunami of debt steals resources from policing so organised illegal tobacco criminals are making billions, recruiting vulnerable kids and making our streets unsafe,” one 30-second Fix Victoria ad says. Bar chart showing the top ten ad spend by political groups ahead of Victoria’s state election ‘Campaign groups exploiting loopholes’ A loophole in Victoria’s electoral laws means voters may never know who is ultimately funding these ads. Groups publishing political ads during campaigns don’t need to be registered as third-party campaigners unless they specifically promote or oppose a party or a candidate. The Centre for Public Integrity’s executive director, Catherine Williams, says Victoria’s laws are narrower in scope than their federal equivalent. “Unless an entity meets the definition of third-party campaigner, no disclosure obligations apply,” Williams says. During the federal election campaign, mandatory donation disclosures by one third-party campaign group revealed it had been bankrolled by the coal lobby . The group had been attacking Labor, Greens and independent candidates. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Transparency International Australia’s chief executive, Clancy Moore, says while Fix Victoria does not meet the legal threshold of a third-party campaign group, its ads are “clearly trying to influence voting”. Pauline Hanson courts wealthy donors with $2,000 ‘exclusive’ Melbourne lunch, but where are the receipts? Read more “It’s really important Victorians know who is behind these types of campaigns and what their political affiliations might be,” Moore says. “There is a long history of third-party and fake grassroots campaign groups exploiting loopholes in electoral laws to try to influence elections.” Rozner says Fix Victoria has “invested considerable resources to ensure strict compliance with all relevant laws, in particular the Victorian Electoral Act”. By avoiding reference to political parties or candidates, Fix Victoria’s financial backers are shielded from public view unless disclosed by the group itself. “We place a very high priority on protecting the security and privacy of our members and supporters,” Rozner says. View image in fullscreen An advertising executive says Fix Victoria spent just under $100,000 on ads in August Better Victoria was formed a month after Fix Victoria, with its first ads running on Facebook in early August. Its political content is endorsed by the group itself, rather than a office holder. Listings with Consumer Affairs Victoria show its secretary is Ronald Holzer, a lawyer based in the Melbourne suburb of Caulfied North. Holzer says he only has an administrative role with the group. He referred a series of questions from Guardian Australia to an unnamed spokesperson, who declined to say who was running the organisation. “Better Victoria has obtained independent legal advice regarding its activities,” the spokesperson said. “It is confident that its activities are fully compliant with Victoria’s electoral laws.” The spokesperson said the group had no relationship with any political party and was fully financed by donations from its members. Those donors will also remain hidden. “Our members include people from a range of backgrounds and professions, who have exercised their right to privacy,” the spokesperson said. ‘They will have spent tens of thousands’ An advertising executive, Ed Coper, who worked with Climate 200 and some teal candidates during the 2025 federal election, says the two groups are spending big. Coper’s agency, Populares, has tracked their spending using public data and says they spent more on Google and Meta ads than any other state election candidate or party in August. He says Fix Victoria spent just under $100,000 on ads, which was about a quarter of all the advertising spend related to the election. Better Victoria spent about $40,000. The two groups also outspent the Liberals, teal independents and One Nation on social media advertising, according to Populares. Then there’s the ad Fix Victoria ran in the middle of the AFL wildcard final between the Western Bulldogs and Collingwood on Channel Seven on 28 August. “They will have spent tens of thousands of dollars,” Coper says. “The actual content of their advertising is very, very similar to the way that a political operative will message during an election campaign.” Explore more on these topics Victorian politics Victoria Social media AI (artificial intelligence) news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story A year after a deadly attack on two boys, Melbourne’s South Sudanese community remains in fear Victoria police confirm they have spoken with four people over Sydney Swans scandal Victorian prisoners to be sent out to repair roads under Labor’s pothole plan Controversial plans for a Daniel Andrews sculpture officially scrapped by Victorian government Levy secretly added to Victorian public transport fares scrapped as Labor admits it ‘did not pass the pub test’ Foster carers in Victoria receive just $231 a week – one quarter the cost of caring for a child Former AFL star Nicky Winmar jailed for six months for assault on woman Victorian government secretly increased public transport fares to help pay for Suburban Rail Loop Liberals criticise ‘unimpressive and underwhelming’ rail loop plan as Victorian premier pushes ahead after hinting at pause Liberal plan to split Victorian appeals court attacked as ‘thought bubble’ that would politicise judiciary Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

( REUTERS ) Summary The country’s fast-paced rearmament is rekindling a century-old debate about how much hard power Berlin should have. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now BERLIN—Germany’s fast-paced rearmament is causing growing concern in Europe, rekindling a century-old debate about how much hard power Berlin should have. The unease is becoming more acute as the Alternative for Germany tops opinion polls. The far-right party, known as the AfD, has embraced Moscow and wants to end what it calls Germany’s “culture of guilt” around its Nazi-era crimes. “We remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,” Poland’s Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, one of the few Polish officials who has long supported a stronger German military, told a German newspaper last week. Days earlier, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the far-left politician currently polling second among candidates in France’s 2027 presidential election, said: “They want to build the largest conventional army in Europe. If I were president, I would tell them that I don’t think that is a good idea.” Just a few years ago, Germany was widely seen as free-riding on the defense budgets of its U.S., French and British allies. President Trump led a chorus of Western leaders pressing Berlin to match military spending with its economic heft. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has since earmarked more than half a trillion dollars for the armed forces over the next decade. Yet some European officials are now beginning to worry that the buildup is shifting the balance of power on the continent. Some fear that even without the AfD, a rearmed Germany and Russia will emerge as the continent’s two biggest powers and Berlin might eventually shift back to accommodating the Kremlin to avoid conflict. Sharpening concerns, Germany’s military procurement has so far benefited mainly German arms-makers. Officials here say they are sensitive to their neighbors’ worries but this has yet to translate into a new approach. This is reminiscent of what historians call “the German question,” a debate among European powers in the 19th century about how powerful a unified Germany could become before it posed a threat to peace. After Germany started two world wars, the answer came: Not too much. Post-World War II Germany was locked into a U.S.-led North Atlantic Treaty Organization. When the Cold War ended, a reunified Germany focused on making money and avoiding military entanglements. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine changed that, kick-starting the biggest rearmament effort on the continent since the the fall of the Berlin Wall. Last year alone, the German government procured defense contracts worth over three times as much as those in the U.K., according to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, an independent think tank. “This is a revolution and it will definitely have an impact on Germany’s neighbors, the EU and trans-Atlantic relationship,” said Lukasz Jasinski, an expert on German-Polish relations at the Polish Institute for International Affairs, a think tank based in Warsaw. “Germany is crucial for European security but it cannot become too big for Europe.” Populists have been particularly strident in articulating these fears. Karol Nawrocki, Poland’s nationalist president, said in a speech this month that Germany didn’t need Hitler to be anti-Polish. The plaudits that greeted Germany’s rearmament drive in 2022 led Berlin to believe it had free rein, said Liana Fix, senior fellow for Europe at the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington. “My perception sometimes was that they had drunk too much of their own Kool-Aid,” she said. Her article “Europe’s Next Hegemon: The Perils of German Power,” which appeared in April in Foreign Affairs, punctured that bubble. The text caught the attention of Merz, who met Fix in Washington earlier this year, according to a German official. The AfD’s electoral victory this month in eastern Germany, where it scored its best result ever, sent another jolt. The party wants Germany to leave the European Union, lift sanctions on Moscow and resume Russian energy purchases. Some of its leaders have questioned NATO’s utility. There has been concern in Poland that a far-right German government would revive old territorial claims against its neighbor. After World War II, Germany lost large chunks of territory that once stretched as far east as Kaliningrad, now part of Russia. More than 12 million Germans were expelled from Eastern Europe. Germany formally renounced these lands upon reunification in 1990, but some AfD leaders have tapped into the loss felt by some expellees. In 2023, AfD Chairwoman Alice Weidel referred to eastern Germany as “Mitteldeutschland,” or central Germany, which some Polish politicians saw as veiled irredentism. Last year, her co-chair, Tino Chrupalla said, “I don’t see any danger to Germany from Russia,” adding that Poland might be a threat. Past chancellors worked hard to keep allies on board. When Helmut Kohl pushed for France and the U.K. to bless reunification, he offered to limit the country’s military. This changed over time. After the eurozone crisis broke out, Angela Merkel imposed German-style fiscal discipline on debt-ridden Greece in exchange for a bailout. When Russia annexed Crimea, she ignored Ukrainian and Polish warnings against opening a second Nord Stream natural gas pipeline linking Germany directly to Russia. Fix said Germany could address the misgivings by binding its rearmament closer to Europe. This could include joint European procurement, more coordination and integration of the defense industry, as well as joint command structures within NATO. It could also agree to a longstanding demand from cash-strapped allies for joint EU-level borrowing to fund defense. Instead, Berlin recently exited multibillion-euro projects with France and the Netherlands. Almost two-thirds of 2025 military spending went to German companies, some 30% went into German production of mainly U.S. systems and close to 10% went outside Europe, according to the Kiel Institute. A tiny amount went to European allies. The concerns about Germany’s buildup are sharpening at a time when the U.S. is planning to downgrade its presence on the continent. Washington often played mediator between European countries with divergent interests and historical grievances. Rym Momtaz, a researcher at Carnegie Europe, said France was concerned about Germany replacing it as a leading military-industrial power. Paris, she added, also believed that Berlin didn’t understand that acting at scale across Europe was the only way to deter attacks on the region. “I think there is widespread nervousness across the French system whether it is political, diplomatic or military about the role that Germany seems to want to give itself,” she said. View full Image The AfD wants Germany to leave the EU, lift sanctions on Moscow and resume Russian energy purchases. In a recent cable seen by The Wall Street Journal, a European diplomat wrote that too often since the start of the war in Ukraine, Berlin was seeing what was good for Germany as necessarily good for Europe. Germany’s allies needed to press Berlin to work with them. Camille Grand, a former assistant secretary-general of NATO, said that some complaints were exaggerated. Germany was engaged in a necessary catch-up, he said, noting that it would have spent an additional $400 billion on defense since 1990 if it had met NATO’s spending target of 2% of economic output. “Germany wants to claim leadership; it isn’t always making great efforts in keeping its partners happy,” he added. Diplomats and analysts doubt that Merz, the most unpopular chancellor in living memory, has enough political capital left to change course. Granting concessions to European neighbors in an effort to make Germany’s rearmament more acceptable to them could even bolster Merz’s nationalist opponents. Wolfgang Ischinger, chairman of the Munich Security Conference and a former diplomat, said rearmament was always going to evoke fears given Germany’s 20th century history. Germany, he added, should reassure its allies that it was aimed solely at meeting NATO and European commitments. “It is not about making Germany great again.” Write to Laurence Norman at laurence.norman@wsj.com and Bertrand Benoit at bertrand.benoit@wsj.com Gift this article Check your portfolio Catch all the Business News , Market News , Breaking News Events and Latest News Updates on Live Mint. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, who Jared Kushner described as ‘a grand master of politics’. Photograph: Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, who Jared Kushner described as ‘a grand master of politics’. Photograph: Getty Images Jared Kushner Analysis Jared Kushner’s 70-minute interview reveals naive bias in handling of Putin’s aggression Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Trump’s son-in-law and senior negotiator paints Russian invasion of Ukraine as a misunderstanding to be resolved Fri 27 Nov 2026 11.49 EST Last modified on Fri 27 Nov 2026 14.34 EST Share In the space of a 70-minute interview, Jared Kushner – Donald Trump’s son-in-law and a prominent US negotiator in Russia, Gaza and Iran – probably did more to reveal why the world is mired in entrenched conflicts than a thousand geopolitical tomes or seminars. During the conversation this week with Mathias Döpfner, the chief executive of the Axel Springer media publisher, Kushner gave a rare insight into his diplomatic technique, offering a string of homilies that veered close to banalities: “You have nothing until you have something”, “diplomacy is like untying knots on a fishing line for his son”, and “you play the ball from where it lands”. There were also many happy admissions of historical ignorance. Since taking on the Ukraine brief a year ago, Kushner said, he had to learn “the algorithm of Europe and how complicated that is”, and he had to get abreast of “the local issues with Ukraine”. View image in fullscreen Jared Kushner, left, stands with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, centre, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff as they speak to the press in Dublin. Photograph: Peter Morrison/AP As a businessman he brought a special expertise, he claimed. “Look at what’s happening in the Middle East with sanctions, with Russia , with Iran. I think that you have to understand economics in order to understand geopolitics because the two go together very, very closely,” he said. But the main revelation was how much he believes the Ukraine conflict is not a case of an aggressor and a victim – but is simply a series of misunderstandings and miscommunication. Indeed, he treated Vladimir Putin as if he were a masterful corporate executive quite willing to close the deal if he were only given the right economic incentives – instead of a man ready to sacrifice hundreds of thousands of Russians to reclaim part of a historical empire . In the process, Kushner revealed – often inadvertently – that he had largely bought into the Russian narrative of a string of postwar missteps by Europe and the US coming to a head in Nato’s expansion eastwards after 9/11. That, in turn, has led him to adopt Moscow’s central demand to reshape the European security order to allow Russia, without opprobrium, to retain land it has gained by force. Shining through his answers was a naive bias towards the aggressor, presented as a mediator’s desire to understand both parties. Praise veering on awe for the Russian leader flowed. “Putin – people can like what he has done, they can not like what he has done – [but] he is a grand master of politics. He is a historic figure,” he said. Any sense that Putin may have blundered escaped him. As to the rights and wrongs of invading another country, Kushner was blasé. “After all, most lines in Europe have changed over time and they are decided through war or peace, or concessions. It’s not about fairness or who is right or wrong. It’s about ending the killing,” he said. He understood, too, why Putin could not offer a ceasefire: “He has very little confidence that if he stops the war, that he [will] be able to get to a postwar settlement that leads to not having a future war.” To stop the killing, the killing has to go on. What is more, Kushner was struck by the Russian leader’s self-control. “So far Putin has shown restraint and he has agreed not to use nuclear weapons and he has reassured us that is his intention.” View image in fullscreen Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin shake hands during a meeting in China. Photograph: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Reuters Kushner denied Trump had put any pressure on Volodymyr Zelenskyy, defying his interviewer to provide evidence – at which point Döpfner recited a list of examples, including only last month when the US president suggested that Ukraine should get a new leader . Trump was “a strong counter-puncher”, argued Kushner, implying that Zelenskyy had thrown the first punch in a conflict that began with a Russian invasion. Relations with Ukraine were cooperative, he said before pointedly saying Kyiv needed things from the US, without which “Ukraine will not be safe in the future”. After noting that “the territorial issue is now a little bit of a deadlock”, his strategic insight was that if a future security architecture for Europe could be agreed, the answer to the land question in Donbas would eventually follow. In essence, he proposed a revival of the Russia-Nato council, one of the bodies eviscerated by Putin’s war. He also envisioned Ukraine inside the European Union with security guarantees akin to those offered by Nato’s article five. Though it was impossible at this stage to give “more specificity” about these guarantees in the detailed way Ukraine sought, he admitted. So far, neither Moscow nor Kyiv have bought this plan, let alone a wary Europe. Kushner tried to be polite about Europe, insisting it had to be at the negotiating table, but he could not stop himself characterising European military assistance to Ukraine as a “proxy war” against Russia. As an analysis of why the Ukraine war had not ended inside the 24 hours Trump had promised when he took office again, Kushner showed an alarming belief that the answer lay in granting more concessions to Putin, and that the misunderstandings and misperceptions would then evaporate.
